**Introduction**  
**Problem Statement**  
Bradford White Corporation (BWC) is seeking a solution for a current problem that they face when testing software releases on their Aerotherm G2 Water Heaters. Each time there is a new software release, they must run quality assurance testing to ensure the water heater unit functions properly. Currently they can only simulate these tests by interacting with a separate user interface that takes data from an external heating test chassis rather than a real unit. They are looking for a device that can automate these tests on fully assembled water heaters, taking real time data from physical units to interact with the user interface. Their intention is to simulate user acceptance testing (UAT) by testing the finished, integrated water heater. They are also looking for the device to be adaptable to future model variations.

**Existing Sponsor Solution**  
Currently, BWC is testing their units using National Instruments software that they have developed and implemented. To “press” buttons and navigate the UI, there are wires soldered to the button pads that simulate the “press” by shorting them using a digital IO unit. The backing of the User Interface (UI) board with the soldered-on wires can be seen in Figure 1 as well as the digital IO unit. 

![][image1]  
**Figure 1\.** Control Board with Soldered Wires and IO unit

Their current solution is not versatile because it requires the desoldering of the testing device, the removal of the faceplate from the test unit, and the resoldering of the testing device, just to be moved from unit to unit. The current solution is also not robust as the NI vision software cannot redefine the borders of the display automatically, thus if the camera gets out of alignment with the display, it needs to be recalibrated. It’s “finicky” to get it right.

The current testing setup does not actually interact with a physical water heater unit, rather it is connected to a heater test chassis, which simulates the water heater's outputs. This is not ideal, as a filled water heater presents different results that may not be detected using the heater test chassis. Due to the inaccuracies in the test chassis the confidence in the current testing setup is relatively low, and removing the test chassis to test directly through the water heater unit is desired. The current testing setup can be seen in Figure 2\. They are using a 3D-printed stand with a 4K webcam to read the screen with the UI PCB mounted underneath. To reduce glare on the screen, a cardboard sheet is placed behind the camera in the designated slot, which helps the vision system get more accurate readings.

![][image2]  
**Figure 2\.** Current Testing Setup

Before the current testing solution, a group of engineers would take shifts to manually press the buttons and wait for the water heater to fill, heat, and drain water from the tank, while also verifying the correct data on the display. To standardize the testing, a large document was created that outlined all the testing steps and expected outputs. This process would take many days and be very costly. The current testing solution is better and more cost effective than the previous, however it still fails to account for the variability that is present when water is being filled, heated, and drained from the tank. It also lacks the factor of repeatability. It is neither portable nor easy to set up.

**Available Solutions**  
A search was conducted to find existing solutions for significant portions of the proposed project, focusing specifically on automated testing fixtures, mechanical button actuation, and screen recognition capabilities.

Companies such as SPEA specialize in automated testing equipment, and have products designed to test a wide range of electronic devices, including keyboards and push buttons. These systems demonstrate adaptability and provide automated button actuation. However, they are designed primarily for stationary benchtop testing rather than for portable use and mounting. Additionally, they are unable to integrate with the user interface of the device. 

Several examples of mechanical button actuation were found in hobbyist-level projects. Each project utilized a different method, including low-cost servos with custom arms, and both electric and pneumatic solenoids. These results provide multiple approaches for button actuation, but they do not incorporate closed-loop feedback through vision-based UI recognition. 

Other online resources and literature were found that address screen text and optical character recognition (OCR). Vision recognition is a well-established topic supported by multiple open source tools. Though they do not address implementation to physical user interface, they show that text recognition can be reliably implemented using a camera. 

Though the individual subsystems of this project exist in current products and literature, there are no available solutions that integrate these capabilities into a portable, adaptable system that interacts with the user interface of an existing appliance using mechanical button actuation and vision recognition. 

**IP Search**  
To verify the boundaries of the proposed solution, an intellectual property search was conducted using Espacenet, focusing on CPC classifications related to testing apparatus (G01M) and actuation mechanisms (H01H). Within these classifications, additional filters were applied to relevant subclasses and keywords, to find patents detailing portable, automated testing fixtures with mechanical actuation that interacts with user interface push buttons. Espacenet did not provide any patents that directly related each requirement.

Google Patents was used for confirmation using a keyword-based search. There were only a few results that showed partial function overlap, but none contained the full requirements of an automated, adaptable fixture with external actuation and user interface capabilities.

**Related Codes & Standards**  
To ensure that the project complies with applicable safety and electrical and mechanical requirements, relevant codes and standards have been identified, reviewed, and curated. These codes and standards will guide our design to prevent potential hazards and ensure safe operation of electrical and mechanical equipment used in the test device. 

**OSHA 29 CFR 1910** establishes occupational safety and health standards for general industry environments such as manufacturing, laboratory, and testing facilities. Subpart S addresses the safe use of electrical equipment and wiring methods, requiring that equipment be clear of hazards such as electrical shock, short circuits, and fire. This standard also stresses that proper insulation and grounding are maintained in the equipment. All electrical components will be UL-listed or otherwise certified for laboratory use. This standard is applicable to the project because the test device functions as electrically powered equipment to be used in a laboratory setting. Compliance with this standard will ensure that electrical hazards associated with the electronic components are taken care of. To verify that this standard is being followed the following tests will be performed. There will be an electrical inspection against the OSHA Subpart S checklist. Continuity tests for grounding will be performed throughout the unit, as well as insulation verification and short-circuit analysis. Finally, all documentation of component certification will be provided.

**ISO 12100** provides a framework for identifying hazards, evaluating the risks of said hazards, and implementing measures to reduce the risk on machinery. The standard addresses a wide range of possible hazards, including mechanical, electrical, functional, and environmental hazards and stresses prioritizing the risks based on severity and likelihood. This standard is applicable to the project since it involves automated mechanical motion and electrical systems which could pose a safety risk during operation. Using ISO 12100 will make sure that potential hazards are addressed to support the goal of producing a safe device. To verify this standard a documented risk assessment table will be provided.

**ANSI B11** focuses on the safeguarding of machinery by identifying mechanical hazards. It also addresses the protection of operators, safeguarding for maintenance, and the use of guards to reduce exposure to hazardous mechanical motion. This standard is applicable to our design in making sure all safety concerns listed are addressed, first the most severe threats, then the others. The risks of our design will lie within the electrical wiring in our design, and the button pressing system. To verify this standard physical measurements of the guard clearances used will be analyzed, a functional test confirming guarded operation will be performed, and all documentation of safeguarding features will be provided.

**IEEE 315-1975** defines standardized graphical symbols used in electrical and electronic schematics. The standard emphasizes the consistency of representation of components in schematics, allowing schematic diagrams to be more clearly understood. This standard is applicable to the project because schematic diagrams will have to be produced of the electrical components of the test device. Following this standard will improve clarity and reduce the risk of misinterpretation of the electrical schematics. To verify this standard all components on the schematics will be compared against the IEEE 315 symbol library, and all schematics will be documented clearly in the final documentation package.

**ASME Y14** establishes the standards for mechanical drawings such as dimensioning and tolerancing. This series of standards ensures that mechanical drawings clearly convey size, shape, and functional relationships between components. This standard is applicable to the project since mechanical drawings will be produced for the test device. Following this standard will aid in making sure the drawings are clear and not ambiguous to the viewer for fabrication. To verify this standard all components on the drawings will be compared against the ASME Y14 checklist, there will be a CAD model cross-check to confirm dimension consistency, and all drawings will be documented clearly in the final documentation package.

**Functional Requirements**  
**General Functional Requirements**  
R-1: The device must include a user manual describing its functions and how to operate it.   
R-2: The device must include an assembly manual that describes how to assemble and build the device. 

**Mechanical Functional Requirements**  
R.M-1: The device must engage with the 7 navigation buttons seen in Figure 3 on the UI.

![][image3]  
**Figure 3\.** User Interface

R.M-2: The device must be portable in weight according to specification \#3 (Table 1).  
R.M-3: The device must be able to mount and dismount from the unit.   
R.M-4: The device must secure itself to the unit for the duration of testing.  
R.M-5: The mounting of the device must not interface with the top of the unit. All mounting must rely on the UI module geometry and/or the sides of the unit.  
R.M-6: The device must be mountable by a single user.  
R.M-7: The device must apply force between the given limits set by specifications \#1 and \#2 (Table 1\) on the UI buttons.

**Electrical Functional Requirements**  
R.E-1: The device must communicate with the control and data acquisition systems.

**Communication and Vision System Functional Requirements**  
R.S-0.1: The communication protocol used must be compatible with the LabVIEW environment.  
→Computer Vision:  
R.S-1.1: The vision system must read dynamic text values from the water heater display.  
R.S-1.2: The vision system must confirm successful navigation of visible menu options.  
R.S-1.3: The vision system must communicate the text/status to the connection interface for the NI control system.  
R.S-1.4: The vision system must provide a method to recalibrate or adjust the region of interest (ROI) used for display detection when the observed display becomes misaligned relative to the light capturing device.  
→Actuation Control:  
R.S-2.1: The control system must accept commands from the testing software to trigger specific button press motion corresponding to the physical user interface (Up, Left, Select, Right, Back, Down, Menu).  
R.S-2.2: The control software must not activate the hold feature when a button is pressed.  
R.S-2.3: The control software must control the actuator engagement to ensure low impact force.

**Use Case Description**

1. Operator picks up the testing device.  
2. Operator attaches the testing device onto the unit, centered on the user interface.  
3. Operator activates power to the testing device.  
4. Operator connects the testing device to the host PC.  
5. Operator starts the testing.  
6. Operator disconnects the testing device from the PC after the testing run concludes.  
7. Operator unclamps the testing device and stores it.

**Needs/Design Constraints**  
**Needs**

1. Closed-Loop Reporting: The system must report the current screen status back to the external NI control system, which performs the actual test verification analysis.  
2. Dynamic OCR Capabilities: The vision system must be capable of reading dynamic text and static menu strings.  
3. Actuation Control: The mechanical interface must replicate human button press interaction, gentle engagement followed by rapid retreat.  
4. Slave Device Operation: The system must operate as a slave device to the existing NI testing infrastructure, accepting low-level physical commands (e.g., “Press Right Button”) and returning the raw observed screen data.  
5. Non-Invasive Mounting: The testing device must attach to the water heater without causing any damage to the water heater or user interface itself. 

**Design Constraints**

1. Budget: The system must be designed and constructed within a total budget of $5,000.  
2. Connectivity Interface: The system must communicate with the host PC via a standard PC interface (Ethernet, USB-B, USB-C) using a protocol compatible with NI LabVIEW.  
3. Physical Geometry: The actuation fingers must align with the button layout of the Aerotherm G2 user interface.  
4. Power Source: The system must operate on independent external power and must not draw power from the water heater’s internal circuitry.  
5. Mounting Physical Compatibility: The mounting mechanism must not rely on the top of the unit. All mounting must rely on the user interface module geometry and/or the sides of the unit.

**Black Box/FSD**  
Figure 4 presents a high-level black box diagram of the test device, describing both its functional inputs and outputs. The test device receives three main inputs: user interface (UI) light which is projected from the display, electricity which is required for operation of the device, and test commands generated by the testing software. These inputs are processed within the black box and produce four main outputs: report data, which communicates the processed results, status, or testing outcomes to an external system, a button press action, which represents the device making actions to control the water heater's user interface, noise which is produced by the button pressing action, and heat which is produced as a part of thermal energy loss. 

![][image4]  
**Figure 4\.** Black Box Diagram

Figure 5 illustrates the function structure of the test device, expanding on the black box diagram and identifying the internal functions. The same inputs and outputs are represented in the function structure diagram with six additional functional blocks linking them. The receive light function captures incoming light from the UI for further processing. The process vision data function interprets the captured light to generate the data that will be reported. The process commands function uses instructions from the testing software to determine the appropriate action for the linear movement function. The linear movement function converts these processed commands into linear mechanical motion, resulting in a button press action. The convert electricity function converts the incoming electrical power to the required operating voltage for the device, and the distribute electricity block supplies this regulated power to the receive light, process vision data, process commands, and linear movement functions. Several of these functions also produce heat as thermal energy loss and generate noise during operation. 

![][image5]  
**Figure 5\.** Function Structure Diagram

**Specifications**  
The design specifications for this project are presented in the numbered list below:

1. The actuation force to press the buttons on the user interface must not exceed 4 lbf when measured with a calibrated force meter. This is to ensure that the buttons are not damaged during testing.   
2. The actuation force to press the button on the user interface must be at least 1.5 lbf when measured with a calibrated force meter to ensure button activation.  
3. The weight of the mountable testing device must not exceed 20 lbs when measured on a scale. This is to ensure ergonomic installation on the water heater, per NIOSH RWL equation.   
4. The cost of the project must not exceed five thousand USD as that is the budget set by BWC.   
5. The time it takes from picking up the device to having it mounted on the water heater must not take longer than five minutes by any team member when measured using a stopwatch.   
6. When mounted, the device shall not move more than ⅛” when subject to an external force less than 5 lbs. Testing will be completed using a force meter to determine the external force subjected to the device and a ruler to measure the movement of the device.   
7. The interface between the test device and the device communicating with it must be a standard PC interface, that is either USB-C, USB-A, USB-B, or ethernet.   
8. The distributed power across the test device must meet the requirements set by each component's data sheet. This is to ensure that each component within the device has the power to operate as intended. To test the power distributed to the components a DMM will be used to measure the voltage.   
9. The button hold down feature must not activate when buttons are pressed. The testing will be done via visual inspection (e.g. temperature set point does not increment by more than 1 degree per button press).  
10. The vision system must accurately detect and report both the dynamic text and static menu strings produced by the display. Testing will be completed by simulating known screen states to read and verify to the external system at a confidence level above 95%.  
11. The mounting must rely on the 6.0625" x 12.6875" UI module and/or the diameter of the unit (22", 26" \- model dependent).  
12. The device must operate exclusively as a slave device within the existing National Instruments (NI) testing infrastructure. The device must accept low-level commands from the master NI controller and return raw data without making decisions. Testing will be completed by inspection of received low-level commands and output raw data.  
13. The vision system must provide a method to recalibrate when the observed display becomes misaligned relative to the light capturing device. Testing will be completed by simulating misalignment and confirming that the recalibration produces accurate results.
